The government should absolutely decriminalize the personal use of recreational drugs. Criminalizing drug use has proven to be a failed policy that disproportionately harms marginalized communities, fuels mass incarceration, and does nothing to address addiction as a public health issue. Punishing individuals for personal drug use only deepens cycles of poverty and trauma, while diverting resources away from effective harm reduction strategies like treatment, education, and safe-use programs.  

Countries like Portugal, which decriminalized all drugs in 2001, have seen significant reductions in overdose deaths, HIV transmission, and drug-related crime. Instead of treating drug users as criminals, they treat addiction as a medical and social issue—and it works. Decriminalization also allows law enforcement to focus on violent crime rather than wasting time on nonviolent drug offenses.  

My stance is rooted in compassion, evidence-based policy, and a belief in personal autonomy. Adults should have the right to make decisions about their own bodies, provided they do not harm others. Criminalization does not stop drug use; it only makes it more dangerous. By shifting to a public health approach, we can reduce harm, save lives, and create a more just society.
